records.title: From close bonds to groups and cultural expectations
records.description: Begin with defined relationships, add physiological and field perspectives, then examine groups, culturally valued feelings and policy aims. The path’s recurring task is to make each change of scale explicit.
records.searchText: Begin with pair bonds and loss, a more specific target than social behaviour in general. Write an operational definition of one relationship outcome. Identify how the definition would need checking when the species changes. Add Carter’s qualified oxytocin hypothesis as a mechanistic proposal. Draw one proposed connection between a physiological measure and your defined outcome. Add a reverse-direction explanation and a potential contextual influence. Introduce field observations and rival accounts of bonding and care. Choose a comparison described in the abstract and list what long-term field observation could reveal that a single laboratory session could not; do not assume it removes every confound. Move to human fatherhood with ecology, culture and family roles explicitly included. Write the same research question for two hypothetical family contexts. Identify a measurement whose interpretation might change between them. Change scale from close relationships to shared identities and collective action. Propose distinct predictions for a shared-identity explanation and an individual-incentive explanation of one fictional cooperative task. Examine an attributed connection between attachment and intergroup processes. Make an evidence request list for the intervention discussed: participants, comparison, outcome, follow-up and rival explanation. Leave effectiveness undecided until those materials are inspected. Add a cultural-emotion perspective, using the inspected Tsai reading and laboratory framework alongside the archive-linked interview. Write separate questions about actual and desired feeling in one fictional setting. Add a within-group variation caution before proposing any cross-cultural comparison. Finish by recognising a transition from explaining social life to choosing collective objectives. Write two paragraphs: one describing an empirical question from the path and one defending a proposed social aim. Underline the value judgement that evidence alone cannot select. No specialist background for the opening steps. Use the linked guides and readings for definitions; advanced modelling steps can be postponed.
terms: Define the relationship or collective outcome being explained.
Separate candidate mechanisms from ecological and cultural context.
Distinguish a report of an intervention from independent evidence of effectiveness.
Separate felt emotion, desired emotion and proposed social objectives.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Comparing minds across species without a single ladder
records.description: Move from scaling and task design to development, field behaviour and human origins. Each step changes one part of the comparison so that the final synthesis is a research plan, not a ranking of species.
records.searchText: Define what a brain comparison is meant to explain before choosing a measurement. Choose a hypothetical ability and list three candidate measurements. Explain what each would leave unmeasured. Add proportional reasoning to the initial measurement question. Use invented size values 1, 2 and 4 with a second measurement 1, 4 and 16. Calculate the changing ratio and label the exercise fictional; explain why it says nothing about real intelligence. Turn from broad anatomical differences to a concrete recognition problem. Distinguish recognising an individual from responding to a familiar signal. Propose one comparison that would help separate those interpretations. Add developmental timing and molecular questions without losing the behavioural target. Make separate boxes for developmental pattern, candidate molecular mechanism and proposed consequence. Mark which link the source identifies as unresolved. Move from a laboratory question to long-term field comparisons and competing explanations. List two explanations of pair bonding or care mentioned in the abstract. State an observation that would be more expected under one than the other. Ask how present comparisons might inform a claim about human origins. Write one potential use and one limitation of a cross-cultural analogy. Identify what historical evidence would still be required. Finish with a deliberately challenging analogy across very different organisms. Construct a one-page comparison plan with separate rows for anatomy, behaviour and organisation. Use the methods reading to identify a confound and an alternative explanation; avoid an overall species score. No specialist background for the opening steps. Use the linked guides and readings for definitions; advanced modelling steps can be postponed.
terms: Distinguish raw size from proportional scaling.
Specify the capacity a behavioural task measures.
Separate developmental mechanism from evolutionary function.
Formulate rival explanations and a discriminating comparison.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: From experience to competing theories of consciousness
records.description: This sequence first clarifies the target, then contrasts workspace, integrated-information and predictive accounts, and finally examines how measures and models enter an empirical test. It does not promise a settled theory of consciousness.
records.searchText: Start with the first-person/third-person problem in Koch’s introductory lesson before comparing proposed answers. Write one question about what is experienced and one question about what an observer could measure. Explain why they are related but not identical. Introduce a clearly named Global Workspace Theory application through VanRullen’s AI discussion. Make two columns: success at an AI task and evidence about experience. Place each claim you identify in one column and write the extra argument needed to connect them. Contrast the workspace-inspired application with Koch’s explicit integrated information proposal. Write the starting commitment of the theory and one observation it would need to explain. Mark which statements are definitions, assumptions or empirical claims. Add Seth’s embodied predictive perspective without substituting it for either of the preceding positions. Identify the aspect of experience or selfhood being explained and formulate one question that would distinguish the explanatory target from the previous two talks. Examine the construction of information-dynamics measures after learning why a theory needs measurements. Create a glossary entry for redundancy and synergy using the source, then state what further argument would be needed before a measure could count as evidence about consciousness. Inspect how a modelling framework and its boundaries can influence an explanation. Draw the system boundary assumed by a model discussed in the abstract. List one process inside, one outside and a reason that changing the boundary could matter. Return to the broader philosophical problem after comparing models and measurements. Use the linked 2025 adversarial-study reading to make a five-column table: theory, preregistered prediction, measurement, result, interpretation. State one unresolved question rather than declaring a winner. No specialist background for the opening steps. Use the linked guides and readings for definitions; advanced modelling steps can be postponed.
terms: Distinguish an experience, a report and a recorded signal.
State the scope of an attributed theoretical proposal.
Construct a comparison of predictions without equating task performance with experience.
Identify assumptions linking a numerical measure or model to a claim.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Design and evaluate a behavioural study
records.description: An eight-step route from a population and outcome to a comparison, power assumptions and an interpretable interval. The associated guide and design readings supply the experimental-design concepts that the statistics demonstrations do not cover.
records.searchText: Begin by separating the people observed from the population the eventual claim concerns. Write a target population and a feasible sample; state one limitation in moving from one to the other. Turn the question into an observation before choosing a statistic. Define the primary outcome, units, time window and variable type. With an outcome defined, narrow the scientific question to a quantity that a statistical comparison can address. State the target difference or proportion in ordinary language and explain what it leaves unanswered. Compare possible target quantities instead of assuming every study concerns an average. Explain why a mean, variability or proportion is the appropriate target for your particular question. Now connect the comparison with the relation between observations. Sketch a separate-group and a paired version; read the linked design chapter and identify a carryover issue. Choose the effect you would want a planned test to detect. Name a meaningful alternative and distinguish it from the null hypothesis. Stress-test the planning inputs rather than reporting one sample-size number. Describe how your plan would change under greater variability or a smaller relevant effect. Finish with the estimate you would report and the uncertainty that should accompany it. Write a mock results sentence with placeholders for an effect estimate and confidence interval, then one sentence about a remaining design limitation. Averages, proportions and simple graphs. Use the probability-review lecture in the uncertainty guide if sampling distributions are unfamiliar.
terms: Specify a population, outcome and target quantity.
Explain why paired and separate-group measurements require different comparisons.
State effect-size and variability assumptions behind a sample-size plan.
Describe the planned estimate and uncertainty without promising a positive result.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Development from behaviour to brain and study design
records.description: Compare two introductory accounts of child development, extend the question across adulthood, then move to cortical organisation and the setting in which developmental studies are conducted. The recurring task is to separate a target ability from the demands of its measurement.
records.searchText: Begin with concrete questions about infancy, learning and cognitive development before moving across explanatory levels. Choose one ability from the session overview. Specify the task used to observe it and another demand that task places on the participant. Compare a second introductory course’s movement from Piaget to infant cognition rather than adopting the first presentation as the only possible framing. Compare how the two lectures formulate a developmental question. Separate the historical theory from the kind of observation used to investigate it. Extend the question into adulthood so that development is considered across the lifespan. Choose an adult-development question and explain whether a task used with younger participants would measure the same thing in the same way. Add cortical organisation as a different level of evidence about developmental change. Write two proposed accounts involving genes and experience. Specify an observation that would help distinguish them for one narrowly defined question. Complete the paired neuroscience discussion and extend its question to change in adulthood. Connect one question from the adult-development lecture to the brain-level discussion while stating what evidence would still be missing. Finish with the practical setting of developmental measurement and who can participate. Using the Lookit description, list a barrier online participation could reduce and a new sampling or measurement question it could introduce. Do not assume wider reach guarantees representativeness. No specialist neuroscience for the first three steps. Review basic brain anatomy before the cortical-organisation lectures.
terms: Describe a developmental question without treating a historical theory as an individual timetable.
Compare behavioural and brain-level observations of change.
Identify task demands and recruitment features that affect interpretation.
Propose an additional comparison that would distinguish explanations of a developmental difference.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Emotion, stress and questions about regulation
records.description: Begin with what an emotional episode contains, compare functional and social explanations, and then study stress and regulation as research questions. The route repeatedly asks what was measured and what would count as a change. It does not promise improved wellbeing or teach a treatment package. The final task turns an appealing regulation claim into an evaluable study question.
records.searchText: Establish the components of emotion before comparing explanations. Describe one fictional episode using separate labels for feeling, activation, bodily change and action. Add an evolutionary perspective to the same explanatory problem. Identify one proposed function and write what evidence would be needed beyond its apparent plausibility. Extend the comparison to social relationships and reciprocity. Ask whether the proposed explanation concerns the individual, an interaction or a broader social pattern. Make measurement explicit before moving to regulation claims. Choose a self-report, behavioural measure and physiological measure; state why they need not be identical observations. Shift from an emotion episode to demands, anticipation and time. Distinguish a stressor, an appraisal or response, and a health outcome in a hypothetical headline. Add the stress course’s named biological component. Record a proposed biological link as a hypothesis and list the observation that would test it. Enter the emotion course’s explicitly named introduction to regulation. Define what is intended to change: a report, behaviour, duration or other outcome. Do not assume all improve together. Finish with variation rather than a universal response recipe. Design a paper-only comparison that specifies population, comparator, outcome and follow-up for a regulation claim. No specialist training; understand the difference between a measured association and an intervention.
terms: Distinguish valence, arousal and a reported feeling.
Compare immediate mechanisms with functional and evolutionary accounts.
Specify a stress measure and its timescale.
Describe what evidence would be needed for a regulation-effect claim.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: From a mental-health claim to an evidence question
records.description: Move from classification and a specific disorder family to treatment evaluation and the difference between individual and population questions. Read the current NIH/NIMH/NICE companions alongside the older lectures. The final product is a hypothetical evidence table or protocol, not a recommendation about care. Each step asks what would support the claim being made and what remains unexplained.
records.searchText: Begin with how difficulties are classified before evaluating interventions for them. Read the NIMH RDoC page and sort one statement each into description, classification, mechanism and treatment outcome. Move from the clinical problem to an accessible historical discussion of treatment approaches; the restricted Yale mood lecture is omitted from the required sequence. Use the current NIMH depression overview to supply present-day context, then write an intervention and intended outcome without assuming its explanation proves effectiveness. Make evaluation the explicit question. Using the NIH trial reading, specify population, comparator, assignment, outcome and follow-up for a fictional study. Separate an outcome comparison from evidence about a biological mechanism. State one neural mechanism that a positive treatment result would still leave open, and the kind of measurement or intervention needed to examine it. Compare a population intervention with an individual-care question. Explain why changing a school or community environment asks a different question from selecting care for one person; finish with the limits of your fictional trial’s generalisation. No clinical qualification; familiarity with the distinction between a description and a causal claim.
terms: Distinguish a diagnostic category from a causal mechanism.
Specify a treatment-evidence question with a population, comparator, outcome and follow-up.
Explain the purpose and limits of random assignment.
Separate individual treatment questions from population-policy questions.
Recognise that a research framework or educational video is not an individual assessment.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: From a study attempt to a teaching design
records.description: Moves from a learner’s retrieval attempt to an educator’s aligned task and feedback design.
records.searchText: Begin with an account of memory before choosing a study technique; this supplies the broader question of what remains available later. Select a concept from the lecture. Write what you can explain now and what a delayed attempt would need to demonstrate. Narrow the question to retrieving long-term information, following the learner’s experience from exposure to a later attempt. Close the source, explain the concept from memory, then reopen it and mark one missing relationship. Do not treat one attempt as an experiment proving a technique’s effect. Metacognition adds a question about judging the attempt: how does a learner know that an explanation is incomplete? Compare your confidence before checking with the specific correction you made. Record the discrepancy without inventing a numerical accuracy score. Move from a learner’s attempt to an educator’s design: constructive alignment connects the intended outcome with the task. Write one objective using an observable verb. Decide whether your recall task actually tests that objective. Keep the implementation lecture beside the principle so that the route produces a concrete design. Draft a practice activity and a later assessment requiring the same kind of reasoning with different examples. Identify one mismatch and repair it. Feedback completes the cycle by connecting evidence from an attempt to what the learner should do next. Write two feedback sentences: identify the actual gap and specify a revision. Explain how you would check whether the revision helped. A small topic to learn or teach; no neuroscience background required.
terms: Separate recognition of an explanation from an attempt to recall it.
Match an observable learning objective with an appropriate practice and assessment.
Write feedback that identifies a specific next action.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Following a movement system from muscle to brain
records.description: Work upwards through the dedicated human-movement course: motor units, spinal circuits and higher systems. The order preserves the relevant official course sequence while omitting unrelated lessons for a manageable first route. Each task adds to one labelled explanation of a hypothetical reach. Anatomical assignments remain tentative until supported; the aim is to connect levels, not memorise a different structure at every stop.
records.searchText: Enter through the dedicated course introduction and its stated scope. Write the movement you want to explain and list its sensory, muscular and timing requirements. Follow the official sequence from muscle foundations to motor units. Add a motor neuron and its supplied muscle fibres to your diagram; keep this separate from a whole-muscle control claim. Locate spinal organisation before the reflex lesson. Mark where sensory information and motor output would enter your diagram, leaving uncertain pathways unlabelled. Use the named monosynaptic-reflex lesson as a focused circuit question. Identify the minimum elements you would need to describe a sensory-to-motor circuit and a measurable response. Reassemble the parts in the course’s motor-control overview. Make a distinction between information available before movement and information available only after movement begins. Extend the overview into the explicitly named primary-motor-cortex sequence. Ask what evidence would support a proposed contribution of cortex; distinguish recording from intervention. Continue into the course’s cerebellum block. Add a question about this system’s contribution, recording the source claim separately from your inference. Compare another higher system instead of assigning all control to one region. Complete a table of structures, proposed contributions and evidence needed. Mark any unanswered question rather than filling it with a familiar slogan. Basic neuron vocabulary; read the course’s membrane and muscle foundations if these are unfamiliar.
terms: Relate a motor unit to neural output and muscle action.
Distinguish preparation, feedback and a local reflex question.
Place spinal, cortical, cerebellar and basal-ganglia topics in one learning map.
State what the inspected course outline can and cannot establish about individual lectures.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: From membranes to interacting circuits
records.description: This route follows the mechanism of communication: charge movement, membrane response, transmission and interacting populations. It differs from a general introduction to computational neuroscience by organising every step around what changes between an input and an output. Begin with conceptual sketches, then use the mathematical and notebook material only as preparation allows. The recurring task is to identify what is measured, what is modelled and what the model omits.
records.searchText: Establish the neuron and nervous-system vocabulary before the physical models. Draw a neuron with input regions, cell body and output. Label this as a simplified diagram, not a complete biological inventory. Move from a labelled cell to the physical sources of current. Explain in separate sentences how a concentration difference and an electrical difference can influence movement of charge. Use the physical account to understand a membrane’s time-dependent response. Sketch a response to a sustained current and mark which features a resistance–capacitance model is intended to represent. Introduce a deliberately reduced spiking model after the circuit foundation. List the threshold/reset rule and two biological details it leaves out. Distinguish a convenient rule from a measured mechanism. Connect cells through transmission rather than treating them as isolated units. Explain why an arrow labelled with a fixed weight may omit saturation, time and input location. Now let a connection’s immediate influence change during activity. Compare a fixed connection with a temporarily changing one under the same hypothetical input train. Distinguish a learning rule from the short-term effects in the preceding step. Write the observation that would be needed to decide whether a change persists beyond the input sequence. Optional advanced branch: combine excitation and inhibition using coupled differential equations after the cell and synapse assumptions. Prepare calculus and phase-plane reasoning, plus linear algebra for stability extensions. Name what the population variables stand for and one single-cell feature that the model does not resolve. Attempt equations/notebooks only with the stated mathematical/Python preparation. For a conceptual skim, use the introductory explanation and descriptive parts of steps 1–4 without attempting derivations. Mathematical study of the ionic/RC and reduced-neuron steps requires algebra, calculus and elementary differential equations. The Wilson–Cowan continuation requires calculus and phase-plane reasoning, with linear algebra for Jacobian/eigenvalue stability work; executing the notebooks requires Python.
terms: Explain why concentration and voltage both matter for ionic current.
Distinguish an observed signal from a reduced model of it.
Separate transmission, short-term synaptic dynamics and a plasticity rule.
Describe what a population model adds to a single-cell explanation.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: What a score says about a person
records.description: Compares performance-based and descriptive measures, then asks what their construction permits us to infer.
records.searchText: Begin with a broad comparison of intelligence and personality so that they are not treated as interchangeable kinds of score. Make two columns for performance tasks and descriptions of characteristic behaviour. Place three possible observations in each. The intelligence session makes testing and competing models explicit. For one task, separate the response, scoring rule, proposed construct and causal explanation. State which steps need further evidence. A dedicated testing lecture provides a focused continuation after the theoretical overview. Invent a scoring rule for three harmless tasks. Explain what consistency would establish and what it would leave unanswered about intended use. Personality changes the focus from task performance to characteristic patterns and their assessment. Describe a fictional person in two settings. Keep the observed behaviour separate from the trait inference. Research methods must come before interpreting associations as explanations. Sketch a design comparing repeated ratings. Identify the rater, context, time interval and one alternative explanation for an association. The five-factor account supplies one influential way to organise trait descriptions, without turning dimensions into fixed types. Choose a broad dimension and two narrower behaviours. Explain how the same broad description could conceal different patterns. Stability and change add time to the measurement question. Describe what data could distinguish stable rank ordering from a change in the average level. State why a one-off score cannot settle either. Basic ideas of an average, variation and repeated measurement.
terms: Separate observed responses, test scores, constructs and causal explanations.
Compare performance tasks with ratings of characteristic behaviour.
Specify what reliability, validity and longitudinal evidence would be needed for an interpretation.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: From neurons and spike data to network models
records.description: Begin with physical and circuit models, connect them to synapses and spike data, then extend to receptive fields and recurrent memory models. Each step asks what the representation includes and what observation would challenge it. This is a selected route, with the full course available for omitted derivations.
records.searchText: Start with the physical ingredients of neuronal currents before replacing them with a simplified mathematical representation. List the ingredients in the opening model and one observation each is intended to help explain. Translate those ingredients into the resistance-and-capacitance representation used by subsequent lectures. Draw the correspondence between a component of the model and the feature it represents. Mark one simplification explicitly. Use the circuit preparation to examine an integrate-and-fire model rather than treating it as an unexplained equation. State what event counts as a model spike and one biological feature the representation does not attempt to reproduce. Add interactions through synapses before proceeding from single-neuron representations to populations and networks. Compare two model situations that differ in synaptic input. Predict a difference and state the assumption behind it. Connect the models to the spike signals and summaries available in recorded data. Specify a data summary and a question it could answer. Describe information that the summary might discard. Now use explicit response models to connect sensory inputs with neuronal activity. Identify the stimulus and response variables in a receptive-field model. Propose a new stimulus that would test its limits. Extend from individual responses to recurrent networks that the course relates to memory and decision-making. Write separately what the network is designed to do and what evidence would be required to treat it as an explanation of a biological system. Finish with attractor memory models and capacity, turning a network’s limits into an explicit object of study. State what the model counts as successful storage or retrieval. Identify a failure condition and explain why it is informative rather than merely inconvenient. Algebra, derivatives, elementary probability and linear algebra. Basic neuroscience vocabulary. For practical follow-up, use the linked Neuromatch Python tutorial; the original MIT problem sets assume MATLAB.
terms: Identify assumptions and omissions in a neuron model.
Relate spike-data summaries to a stated modelling question.
Describe how response and recurrent-network models address different problems.
Separate fitting or generating a behaviour from validating a biological explanation.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: From a brain question to an experiment
records.description: Follow the Human Brain course from its central questions through methods, experimental design and competing interpretations. The route preserves the relevant lecture order and adds a continuing task: refine one question into two discriminating experiments.
records.searchText: Begin with the course’s aims so that the methods are attached to questions rather than learned as a list of technologies. Write one question about cognition that you would like evidence to answer; distinguish it from a general topic such as “vision”. Now compare the range of methods the course introduces for investigating those questions. Make a four-column table: question, measured quantity, comparison and remaining uncertainty. Add two methods from the lecture. Complete the methods pair before choosing an approach for your own question. Add another approach and describe what complementary observation it could provide. Avoid claiming that one method settles every part of the question. Move from recognising methods to constructing an experimental comparison, using the course’s face-recognition context and design brief. Read the linked experimental-design assignment. Sketch two linked experiments: the second should challenge an explanation still compatible with the first. Use a domain with explicit competing interpretations to test whether your proposed comparisons could distinguish accounts. For two possible accounts, state a different prediction. Identify which observation would leave the accounts unresolved. Finish by extending the question from local organisation to relationships between regions. Rewrite one network claim to specify the evidence it would need. Identify an anatomical, statistical or task-related ambiguity you would investigate next. Introductory psychology and willingness to learn basic neuroscience terminology. Review brain anatomy separately if the course’s regional vocabulary is unfamiliar.
terms: Describe a study in terms of question, task, measure and comparison.
Explain why different methods bear on different aspects of a question.
Propose a follow-up experiment that tests an alternative explanation.
Distinguish a relationship between brain regions from a complete account of their interaction.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Read a quantitative paper critically
records.description: A ten-step reading sequence that moves from the recorded variables and descriptive patterns to the tested parameter, uncertainty, model assumptions and prediction claims. Use the linked causal and transparency readings for questions the statistical calculation cannot answer.
records.searchText: Start with what the paper actually recorded, before reading its conclusion. List each main variable, how it was obtained and the proposed interpretation. Check who or what contributes to each percentage. Write the numerator, denominator and missing-data count for one reported proportion, or mark the missing information. Add spread to the reported centre. Find a spread measure and state whether it describes individual variation or uncertainty in an estimate. Inspect the pattern before accepting a single association summary. Sketch what the scatterplot would need to reveal, including unusual points or separate groups. Identify which kind of parameter the analysis tests. Decide whether the reported test concerns a mean, a variance or a proportion; record its assumptions rather than guessing from the p-value. Interpret the p-value as a conditional calculation. Rewrite the p-value sentence without assigning a probability that the hypothesis is true. Relate the test to the effect estimate and matching interval. State which effect sizes remain compatible with the reported uncertainty under the chosen method. Inspect the statistical model behind a coefficient. List the outcome, predictors and one error-model assumption; label a causal claim separately. Separate fitting the observed data from predicting new observations. Identify whether an interval refers to a fitted mean or a new case, and what evidence of out-of-sample performance is available. Return to the sampling model that makes the inference meaningful. Write a five-sentence appraisal: observation, estimate, uncertainty, assumption and unresolved reporting item. Consult TOP before claiming the result is reproducible. Comfort with simple graphs and averages. Basic probability is useful for the later inference steps.
terms: Identify the recorded variables, denominators and target quantity.
Distinguish effect size, p-value and interval uncertainty.
Recognise when a regression claim changes from association to prediction or causation.
Write a concise assessment with explicit unresolved information.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Sleep, hunger and the circumstances of motivation
records.description: Start with Sleep 3, whose official description concerns rhythms and sleep, and the accompanying NIGMS reading; then compare emotion and eating. Sleep 1/2 are omitted from the required sequence because their descriptions discuss consciousness and appear inconsistent with their titles. The route is organised around regulation, cues and measurement, ending with food access so that an explanation of a choice remains connected to its circumstances.
records.searchText: Use the lesson whose actual publisher description names biological rhythms, sleep and polysomnography. The API title matches; Sleep 1/2’s inconsistent descriptions are not used to infer content. Read NIGMS first, then write separate questions about sleep timing, measurement and mechanism. Mark any lecture claim that the reading does not establish. Introduce a vocabulary for affect and motivation before considering food. Distinguish pleasantness from activation in two invented examples; do not treat either as a complete measure of hunger. Move into a concrete biological and behavioural research setting. Write one question about taste, one about eating behaviour and one about body weight, noting that they are different outcomes. Check the measurement problem before interpreting models. Compare what an intake recollection, a laboratory choice and an availability record could each establish. Examine an addiction-model perspective as a testable account. State one observation the model would need to explain and an alternative account to distinguish; do not diagnose a person. End with access and economics so that internal-state explanations are not isolated from available options. Design a hypothetical comparison separating stated preference from price and availability. Identify the causal uncertainty that remains. No specialist neuroscience; read the NIGMS circadian fact sheet before the first step. The source-description inconsistency is a reason to keep the clock reading distinct from unverified video content.
terms: Distinguish a daily behavioural pattern from a proposed clock mechanism.
Separate an internal state, a cue and an observed action.
Identify measurement uncertainty in eating research.
Compare an individual reward model with an environmental-access explanation.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: A first route through strategic interaction
records.description: Preserves order within Yale’s course while selecting a bridge from simultaneous choice to timing, information and repetition.
records.searchText: Begin by distinguishing an outcome from its value to each player, using the course’s classroom games. Construct a two-player table with explicit outcomes and payoffs. Change a player’s preferences while keeping the physical outcomes fixed. Reasoning about another player introduces assumptions about their information and expectations. Write what each player knows and believes in your example. Identify a conclusion that needs more than each player knowing only their own payoff. Iterated deletion turns those assumptions into a procedure and a model of electoral competition. Mark one dominated strategy in a small table, if one exists. Explain what additional assumption is needed before deleting another player’s strategy in response. Best responses connect a specified belief about another action to the player’s own choice. For each possible opposing action, identify a best response. Keep ties visible rather than forcing a single answer. Nash equilibrium asks whether the players’ choices are mutually consistent best responses. Find the equilibria of your table. Separately ask which outcome each player prefers; explain why these are different questions. Sequential games add timing and later opportunities to revise a choice. Draw a short decision tree and work backwards. Mark one threat that the player would not want to carry out when its turn arrived. Information sets show why moves occurring in order need not mean the later player knows the earlier action. Compare two trees with identical available actions but different information. Identify which inference from backward reasoning needs reconsideration. Repeated games add future consequences, making the stopping rule a key part of the model. Compare a known final round with uncertain continuation. Write what would make a promised future response credible under each arrangement. Yale states introductory microeconomics as a prerequisite, uses mainly one-variable calculus and refers to probability and expectation. A small payoff-table exercise can be attempted first, but the full route is mathematically more demanding than a general-interest talk.
terms: Identify players, actions, outcomes and payoffs separately.
Find best responses and explain why equilibrium need not be desirable.
Show how timing, information and repetition alter the model of a choice.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Studying change from adolescence to ageing
records.description: Compare two transitions rather than surveying every stage of life. The first half asks how biological change, peers and media settings are studied; the second asks how cognitive outcomes and theories of ageing are distinguished. Repeated tasks separate group differences from within-person change. This route is about the logic and scope of developmental claims, not a timetable for judging individuals.
records.searchText: Revisit how developmental theories and milestones are introduced before examining later transitions. Identify one question about a capacity and another about how that capacity was measured. Use a clear older account of adolescent novelty seeking as a claim to assess. Compare the publisher’s framing with the NIMH teen-brain reading; avoid turning an average trend into an individual prediction. Introduce a contemporary example of measurement and reciprocal person–environment relationships. In the inspected early-childhood example, distinguish the child, caregiver, setting and measured media use; state why it is not direct adolescent evidence. Bridge the transition to adult-development methods and cognitive/emotional change. Explain what comparing different ages can show and what following the same people adds. Specify memory systems before using a memory task as an ageing outcome. Name two tasks that make different demands and explain why clinical amnesia is not a model of ordinary ageing. Examine the evaluative language of successful ageing. List three possible valued outcomes and explain why a person’s worth cannot be reduced to one of them. Add a biological level without treating it as a complete account of cognitive performance. Draw separate boxes for biological mechanism, task performance and life circumstances, and identify evidence needed for each proposed link. An introductory account of child development; basic understanding of an observational study.
terms: Separate developmental averages from predictions about individuals.
Distinguish peer selection and influence as alternative explanations.
Separate cognitive outcomes, biological mechanisms and valued outcomes in ageing.
records.provider: Evidence Press

records.title: Probability models and human judgement
records.description: Establishes mathematical standards before considering judgements and selection effects.
records.searchText: Begin with the rules and objects of a probability model so that later comparisons have an explicit standard. Make a sample space for a fictional draw from a box. State what the model assumes about the draw and what it leaves out. Conditioning adds information to that model rather than replacing the model with an intuitive story. Make a table of counts for two colours and a noisy label. Calculate the colour probability after observing the label; then change the base rate. Independence is a distinct assumption, often hidden in informal probability arguments. Write what independence would mean for two events in your example. Identify a plausible change to the draw that would make the assumption fail. With a comparison rule available, examine human problem solving, heuristics and framing. Choose a puzzle and state the intended rule, the information provided and the response. Explain which claimed error actually follows from those premises. Gendler adds sampling and philosophical questions, showing why a description of reasoning needs more than a list of bias names. Distinguish a sampling problem from a disagreement over values. Give one example of each and identify what would resolve it. The auction example applies conditioning to selection: learning that one won can itself be informative. Describe what the event of winning reveals in the lecture’s model. State one changed assumption under which the inference would differ; do not turn the exercise into bidding advice. Fractions, basic algebra and set notation for the opening work. MIT’s full probability course requires a year of college-level calculus; the Yale auction continuation also belongs to a course requiring introductory microeconomics.

Compute a conditional probability and recognise an independence assumption.
Separate an error relative to a specified model from a disagreement about goals or modelling choices.

records.title: From recognising words to understanding sentences
records.description: Tracks linguistic units and processing questions from words through structure to discourse.
records.searchText: Start with a broad account of language so that sound, word, structure and meaning are available as separate questions. Make four columns: signal, word, sentence and context. Place one question from the lecture in each. The lexical-access sequence narrows the route to how relevant word knowledge becomes available. Choose a familiar word and distinguish its form, meaning and grammatical use. State what a recognition task would ask a participant to do. Continue the same course’s lexical-access treatment before moving to larger units. Compare recognising the word with trying to produce it. Specify what would count as an error in each task. Now make the sentence the unit of analysis, while retaining the distinction between structure and processing. Write a sentence whose final phrase could modify two different things. Give the two interpretations without yet claiming how a listener chooses. The first parsing lecture begins the course’s explicit sequence on assigning structure during comprehension. Draw or paraphrase the two structural analyses. State one observation that a proposed processing account would need to explain. The second parsing lecture provides continuity rather than a disconnected overview of the same label. Write two competing predictions about when ambiguity might affect a response. Identify the task and comparison needed to distinguish them. Discourse changes the scale from one sentence to connected communication and shared context. Add a preceding sentence that favours each interpretation. Explain what the context changes and what structural ambiguity remains. Basic familiarity with a word, a phrase and a sentence; no brain-imaging knowledge required.
terms: Separate a linguistic unit from a process that makes it available.
Represent two structural interpretations of the same sentence.
Explain what context adds beyond word meanings and sentence structure.
